title: I Found The Perfect Way To Cook TJ's Gyoza (And It's Not In The Instructions) - NewsBreak
text:
By Bay Nigro ,
21 hours ago
I’m going on 13 years of loving Trader Joe’s gyoza and potstickers. From the Veggie and Chicken Potstickers to the Thai Shrimp and Vegetable Gyoza, I always keep a bag in the freezer when the craving calls. They’re easy to throw into soup, serve over rice, or pair with noodles, making them a great shortcut for weekday dinners. I’ve usually just cooked them in a skillet with a little oil (gyoza purists, please forgive me), but recently I read the back of the bag and realized there are actually a few different ways to prepare them. There’s the classic pan-fry-steam-fry method (aka yaki gyoza ), traditional steaming, and even oven-baking, which I kept seeing online. I realized I’d been cooking them differently than intended all along, which made me wonder how much the method actually changes the final result. Nick & Bay Nigro So, to do a bit of first-hand culinary research, I took a bag of Trader Joe’s Thai Shrimp Gyoza and cooked equal batches three different ways: pan-fry-steam-fry (according to the package), steamed (also according to the package), and oven-baked (the wild card). I paid close attention to texture (crispy versus soft), flavor, cook time, and how much effort each method required. Here’s how it went. What I Used:
1 bag Trader Joe’s frozen Thai Shrimp Gyoza
Neutral oil
Water
Tools:
Nonstick skillet with lid
Steamer basket
Sheet pan + parchment paper
Nick & Bay Nigro Related: "21 Forgotten Food Trends From The '70s And '80s"
Method 1: Pan-Fry-Steam-Fry This is the classic gyoza method, and the one I assumed would be my favorite. I heated oil in a skillet, added the gyoza flat-side down, and let them cook until the bottoms were golden. Then I added water, covered the pan, and let them steam before removing the lid to finish. Time: About 10 minutes
Effort: Medium (you have to stay nearby and monitor)
Nick & Bay Nigro Method 1: Results These were delicious right away. The wrappers had that slightly chewy, tender texture, and the filling stayed juicy. The bottoms started crispy, but the steaming step softened them slightly, which is what you want with this method (though not exactly the texture I tend to go for). This method is classic for a reason, especially if you like that balance of tender and lightly crisp, but it wasn't the crispiest option overall.
Nick & Bay Nigro Related: "21 Cooking Skills That Even Seasoned Home Chefs Can't Master"
Method 2: Steamed I’m not usually a steamer-type when it comes to food, but this felt like the simplest, most straightforward approach. I placed the gyoza in a steamer basket over simmering water and steamed them until heated through. Time: About 10 minutes
Effort: Low
Nick & Bay Nigro Method 2: Results Related: "Tell Us The Worst Halloween Candy That Haunted Your Childhood"
These were very soft with delicate wrappers. That said, they stuck slightly during steaming and ended up being the soggiest of the three methods. They're soft and perfectly cooked inside, but missing the crispy contrast that I personally love in gyoza. Nick & Bay Nigro Method 3: Oven-Baked This was the method I was least confident about, but it ended up being my favorite! I lightly coated the gyoza in oil, arranged them on a parchment-lined sheet pan, and baked them at 400°F for about 15 minutes, rotating the pan halfway through. Time: About 15–18 minutes
Effort: Very low (no active monitoring)
Nick & Bay Nigro Method 3: Results These had the best crisp of all three methods. The wrappers were golden and slightly firm, while the filling stayed tender inside. They were also by far the easiest to cook, with no flipping, no covering, and just a quick rotation of the tray. Crispy, low-effort, and (for my personal preference) the tastiest overall. These would also be fab for entertaining.
Nick & Bay Nigro Related: "33 New Costco Fall Items Flying Off Shelves Right Now"
Final Thoughts I went into my experiment expecting the skillet method to prevail, but the oven version ended up being my favorite. That being said, I do want to revisit the pan-fry-steam-fry method a few more times. It’s the traditional approach, and I know there’s a technique to getting that ideal crisp-to-tender balance. Of course, a lot of this comes down to personal preference. I love things crispy, so it makes sense that I gravitated toward the oven method. But if you love a softer, more classic dumpling wrapper, the steamed or skillet versions might be more your style. Nick & Bay Nigro TL;DR: For the crispiest result, go with the oven. For the most classic texture, stick with the skillet. For a softer, more delicate dumpling, steaming works best. Nick & Bay Nigro I’d love to hear your go-to method or any creative ways you serve these delightful little dumplings. And if you grew up eating them, I’m especially curious to hear how your family made them. Any tips or traditions you swear by to achieve ultimate gyoza goodness?
